title: Deadlocks and classic synchronisation problems
scopeHtml: Scope: Coffman conditions, prevention, avoidance, detection, producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers and real hangs. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: What a deadlock is
notes.html:
A deadlock is when a group of threads each wait for something another in the group holds, so none can ever move. No crash, no error, no CPU use. The service just stops answering and thread count climbs.

Smallest example: thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2; thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1.

// Thread 1                          // Thread 2
synchronized (a) {                   synchronized (b) {
    synchronized (b) { ... }             synchronized (a) { ... }
}                                    }

Worked example. A transfer function locks the source account then the destination. Alice sends to Bob while Bob sends to Alice at the same moment: T1 locks Alice, T2 locks Bob, T1 waits for Bob, T2 waits for Alice. With 5,000 transfers/s over 1 million accounts, the chance that two opposite transfers overlap is small but not zero, so it fires once a week in production, usually at peak.

How to see it in production.

$ jstack 2310
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"transfer-12":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f2c (object 0x000000076ab1, a Account),
  which is held by "transfer-7"
"transfer-7":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f2d (object 0x000000076ab2, a Account),
  which is held by "transfer-12"

For native programs: gdb -p PID -batch -ex "thread apply all bt" and look for many threads in __lll_lock_wait / futex_wait. Symptoms in metrics: throughput drops to zero while CPU is near idle, thread pool queue grows, health check times out.

Industry examples. MySQL InnoDB and Postgres detect row-lock deadlocks and kill one transaction (ERROR 1213 Deadlock found / deadlock detected), so apps must retry. Java's ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() is used by monitoring agents.

Everyday analogy. Two cars meet on a single-lane bridge, each waiting for the other to back up.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up deadlock (waiting forever, no CPU) with livelock (running but making no progress) and starvation (one thread never gets served).
  • Thinking a deadlock needs locks only. It can involve semaphores, DB rows, file locks, or a thread pool waiting on its own queue.

notes.title: The four Coffman conditions
notes.html:
A deadlock can happen only if all four conditions hold at once. Break any one and deadlock is impossible. Coffman listed them in 1971.

  1. Mutual exclusion: a resource can be held by only one thread at a time.
  2. Hold and wait: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another.
  3. No preemption: a resource cannot be taken away by force; the holder must release it.
  4. Circular wait: a cycle exists: T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T3, ..., Tn waits for T1.
Condition How to break it Cost
Mutual exclusion Make the resource shareable (read-only data, lock-free, immutable) Not always possible (a printer, a row being updated)
Hold and wait Take all locks at once, or release everything before waiting Lower concurrency, risk of starvation
No preemption Use tryLock with timeout and back off (give up what you hold) Need retry logic; livelock risk
Circular wait Global lock ordering Needs discipline across the codebase; cheapest

Worked example (the resource-allocation graph). Draw threads as circles and resources as squares. Edge R -> T means T holds R; edge T -> R means T waits for R. With one instance of each resource, a cycle in the graph means deadlock. With several instances per resource, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.

Decision gravity. In practice 95% of deadlocks are fixed by breaking circular wait with an ordering rule, because it is free at runtime and easy to review. Hold-and-wait removal hurts throughput. Preemption works for databases (abort a transaction, roll back) but is hard for in-memory locks.

Everyday analogy. Four cars at a crossroads each waiting for the car on their right: all four conditions hold (road space is exclusive, each holds its spot while wanting the next, nobody can be pushed, and they form a circle).

Common interview traps.

  • Listing the conditions but not saying "all four needed, so removing one is enough".
  • Claiming a cycle always means deadlock; with multiple resource instances it may not.

notes.title: Prevention
notes.html:
Prevention means designing the code so that at least one Coffman condition can never hold. It costs nothing at runtime if done by convention, so it is the first line of defence.

1. Lock ordering (breaks circular wait). Give every lock a rank; always acquire in increasing rank. For transfers, order by account id.

void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    Account first  = from.id < to.id ? from : to;
    Account second = from.id < to.id ? to   : from;
    synchronized (first) {
        synchronized (second) {
            from.balance -= amt; to.balance += amt;
        }
    }
}

2. Try-lock with timeout (breaks no-preemption and hold-and-wait).

if (a.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
  try {
    if (b.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
      try { work(); } finally { b.unlock(); }
    } else { /* back off: release a, sleep random 1-20 ms, retry */ }
  } finally { a.unlock(); }
}

Add random back-off or two threads retrying in lock-step produce a livelock.

3. Acquire everything up front, or use one coarse lock. Simplest and often right below a few thousand ops/s.

4. Do not call unknown code while holding a lock (callbacks, listeners, Object.equals of user types). The hidden callee may take another lock in the opposite order.

Linux kernel practice. The kernel documents lock order in comments and uses lockdep (CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING) to learn the acquisition graph at runtime and warn about potential cycles before they ever deadlock. Output looks like WARNING: possible circular locking dependency detected. In user space, Clang's thread-safety annotations and TSan's deadlock detector do similar checks.

Industry examples. Postgres orders buffer-lock acquisition rules; MySQL advises to access tables and rows in the same order in every transaction. Go has no lockdep, so teams use go-deadlock in tests.

Everyday analogy. Numbering all tools in a shared workshop and agreeing "always pick up the lower number first": no two people can ever each hold what the other needs.

Common interview traps.

  • Ordering by memory address works but hides intent; ordering by stable id is clearer. Not handling from == to (locking the same object twice) is a real bug.
  • Using tryLock without back-off or a retry limit.
  • Thinking Java synchronized can time out. It cannot; use ReentrantLock.tryLock.

notes.title: Avoidance and the Banker's algorithm
notes.html:
Avoidance means the system grants a request only if it keeps the state "safe", meaning some order exists in which every thread can finish. It needs to know each thread's maximum future needs in advance.

Banker's algorithm (Dijkstra). Think of a bank with limited cash and customers with credit limits. Before lending, check: after this loan, could the bank still pay out so everyone eventually finishes? If yes, the state is safe and the loan is granted; if not, the borrower waits.

Worked example. 12 units of one resource. Maximum needs and current holdings: P1 max 10 holds 5, P2 max 4 holds 2, P3 max 9 holds 2. Free = 12 - 9 = 3.

  • P2 needs 2 more; 3 free, so P2 finishes and returns 4, so free becomes 3 - 2 + 4 = 5.
  • P1 needs 5 more; free is 5, so P1 finishes and returns 10. Free = 10.
  • P3 needs 7 more; free is 10, so it finishes. Safe sequence: P2, P1, P3. If P3 had asked for 1 more earlier and the system had only left 2 free, no sequence might exist and the request would be delayed.

Why almost no real OS uses it. It needs advance maximum claims (applications do not know them), a fixed number of threads, and the check is O(m x n^2). Real systems prefer prevention by ordering, or detection and recovery. Avoidance does appear in embedded and real-time systems with static task sets, and in a lighter form: admission control (limit the number of transactions or connections so resources cannot be exhausted).

Decision gravity. Avoidance is conservative (it refuses some safe requests, lowering utilisation) and complex; prevention and detection are chosen in practice. Reversible but rarely worth it.

Everyday analogy. A bank manager who refuses a loan if it would leave no money for the remaining customers to ever complete their projects.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing a safe state with "no deadlock right now". An unsafe state may still not deadlock; it just can.
  • Saying Linux uses the Banker's algorithm. It does not.

notes.title: Detection and recovery
notes.html:
Detection lets deadlocks happen, finds them, and breaks them. It suits systems where deadlocks are rare and a victim can be rolled back, mainly databases.

How to detect. Keep a wait-for graph: node per transaction, edge T1 -> T2 if T1 waits for a lock T2 holds. A cycle is a deadlock. Run a cycle search (depth-first) periodically or when a wait exceeds a threshold.

How to recover.

  1. Kill a victim: pick by cheapest rollback (fewest rows changed, youngest, lowest priority), abort it, release its locks.
  2. Preempt and roll back to a savepoint.
  3. Avoid starvation: do not always choose the same victim; count how many times a transaction was picked.

Real databases.

  • InnoDB: checks the wait-for graph immediately on lock wait (innodb_deadlock_detect=ON by default). Picks the transaction with the least changed rows. With very hot rows, detection itself becomes costly (many waiters); some set innodb_deadlock_detect=OFF and rely on innodb_lock_wait_timeout (default 50 s; lower it).
  • PostgreSQL: waits deadlock_timeout (default 1 s) before running detection, then aborts one with ERROR: deadlock detected and shows both statements in the log.
mysql> SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
------------------------
LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK
------------------------
*** (1) TRANSACTION: ... UPDATE accounts SET bal=bal-10 WHERE id=1
*** (2) TRANSACTION: ... UPDATE accounts SET bal=bal+10 WHERE id=2
*** WE ROLL BACK TRANSACTION (2)

The app must catch the error and retry the whole transaction (usually 3 attempts with jitter).

In-process detection. JVM: jstack or ThreadMXBean. Watchdog thread that timestamps lock waits and dumps stacks after 10 s. Kubernetes liveness probes will restart a deadlocked pod after e.g. 3 failed checks, which hides the bug: always capture a thread dump before the restart.

Industry examples. Oracle and SQL Server also kill victims (SQL Server error 1205). Google Spanner uses wound-wait to avoid deadlocks: an older transaction "wounds" (aborts) a younger one that holds a needed lock, and a younger one waits for an older one.

Everyday analogy. A traffic marshal who spots a gridlocked junction and orders one car to reverse out.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the application retry. The DB aborting is normal behaviour, not a bug in the DB.
  • Not mentioning that detection costs CPU and can itself be a bottleneck under heavy contention.

notes.title: Producer-consumer
notes.html:
Producers create items, consumers process them; a bounded buffer sits in between so the two sides run at different speeds. Producers must wait when the buffer is full, consumers must wait when it is empty, and access to the buffer must be exclusive.

Classic solution with three semaphores: empty (starts at N, free slots), full (starts at 0, filled slots), and mutex (1, protects the buffer).

producer:                   consumer:
  wait(empty)                 wait(full)
  wait(mutex)                 wait(mutex)
  buffer.put(item)            item = buffer.take()
  signal(mutex)               signal(mutex)
  signal(full)                signal(empty)

Swap the first two waits in either side (take mutex before empty/full) and you get a deadlock: a producer holds the mutex while sleeping on empty, consumers can never get the mutex to free a slot.

BlockingQueue<Job> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000);
// producer: q.put(job);    blocks when full  (back-pressure)
// consumer: Job j = q.take(); blocks when empty

Worked example. Producers make 5,000 jobs/s, consumers process 3,000 jobs/s. An unbounded queue grows 2,000 jobs/s: at 1 KB each that is 2 MB/s, so 7 GB per hour until OOM. A bounded queue of 1,000 forces producers to block (back-pressure), and the speed mismatch becomes visible instead of fatal. Choosing the bound: about (peak burst length x rate difference). Alternatives when blocking is unacceptable: drop, shed load with 429, or spill to disk/Kafka.

Industry examples. Kafka is a durable distributed producer-consumer log. Java ThreadPoolExecutor has a work queue; Go channels (make(chan Job, 1000)) are bounded queues; Linux pipes are 64 KB kernel buffers (the writer blocks when full).

Everyday analogy. A kitchen pass: chefs put plates on a shelf with 10 spots, waiters take them. A full shelf stops the chefs; an empty one makes the waiters wait.

Common interview traps.

  • Unbounded queues. They hide overload until memory is gone; always state the bound and the full-queue policy.
  • Wrong semaphore order. Say why it deadlocks.
  • Not handling shutdown: use a poison-pill item or close the channel so consumers exit.

notes.title: Readers-writers
notes.html:
Many readers can read together; a writer needs exclusive access. It is common (config, caches, routing tables). The problem is policy: who wins when both wait?

  • Readers-preference: new readers join while a reader is active. High read throughput, but a steady stream of readers starves writers.
  • Writers-preference: once a writer waits, new readers queue behind it. Fixes writer starvation, may slow readers.
  • Fair (FIFO): requests served in arrival order. Predictable, less parallel.
ReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true /* fair */);
String get(String k) { rw.readLock().lock();  try { return m.get(k); }  finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } }
void   put(String k, String v) { rw.writeLock().lock(); try { m.put(k, v); } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } }

Worked example. A read takes 1 microsecond and a write 100 microseconds; 1,000 reads/s per thread across 16 threads and 10 writes/s. A plain mutex serialises all reads; the RW lock lets 16 readers run together. But the RW lock itself is a shared counter: every readLock is an atomic update on one cache line, so on many cores the readers still bounce that line. The read path then costs 50 to 200 ns instead of 20 ns.

Better options for read-mostly data.

  • Copy-on-write: writer builds a new copy and swaps one pointer atomically (CopyOnWriteArrayList, Go atomic.Value). Readers take no lock at all. Fine when writes are rare and data is small.
  • RCU (read-copy-update): the Linux kernel's way; readers run lock-free, the writer publishes a new version and frees the old after all readers have passed a grace period. Used for routing tables, dentry lookup.
  • Java StampedLock with optimistic reads: read, then validate no write happened; retry if so.
  • Sharding: ConcurrentHashMap.

Decision gravity. RW locks are often not worth it: if writes exceed roughly 10% of operations or critical sections are tiny, a plain mutex wins. Reversible if abstracted.

Everyday analogy. A library reading room: many people read the same notice board at once, but to repaint it everyone must leave.

Common interview traps.

  • Upgrading a read lock to a write lock while holding it: deadlocks in ReentrantReadWriteLock (it does not support upgrade). Release and reacquire, then re-check.
  • Not naming the starvation trade-off.
  • Assuming RW locks are always faster than mutexes.

notes.title: Dining philosophers
notes.html:
Five philosophers sit at a round table, one fork between each pair; to eat, a philosopher needs both adjacent forks. It is the textbook model for deadlock and starvation among threads sharing overlapping resources.

Naive: everyone picks up the left fork, then the right. If all five pick up their left fork at the same time, each waits forever for the right one. All four Coffman conditions hold.

Solutions, each breaking a condition:

  1. Resource ordering (break circular wait): number the forks 0 to 4; always pick the lower-numbered fork first. The last philosopher (forks 4 and 0) picks 0 first, so the cycle cannot close. Simple and starvation-light.
  2. Limit to N-1 diners with a counting semaphore of 4: at least one philosopher can always get both forks.
  3. Waiter / arbitrator (single mutex): ask a waiter for permission to take both forks at once (breaks hold-and-wait). Reduces parallelism.
  4. Chandy-Misra: forks are "clean" or "dirty" and passed by request; decentralised and starvation-free (used in distributed settings).
  5. Try-lock and back off: pick left, try right with timeout, put left down if it fails. Risk of livelock without randomisation.
// Solution 1: order by fork id
int a = Math.min(left, right), b = Math.max(left, right);
forks[a].lock(); forks[b].lock();
try { eat(); } finally { forks[b].unlock(); forks[a].unlock(); }

Worked example. 5 philosophers, eat time 10 ms, think time 10 ms. Max parallel eaters is 2 (5 forks / 2 per eater, floor). Ordering gives about 2 concurrent eaters most of the time; the "N-1 diners" semaphore also reaches 2; the single-waiter solution gives 1. So throughput rank: ordering ~ semaphore > waiter.

Real-world mapping. A thread needing two locks (transfer between accounts), a database transaction updating two rows, or a worker needing two connections from two pools. The solution is always: global order, or take both together.

Everyday analogy. Five people at a table sharing chopsticks: if everyone grabs the left stick, all starve politely.

Common interview traps.

  • Offering "the philosopher waits a random time" as a fix without noting it does not guarantee progress.
  • Forgetting starvation: ordering prevents deadlock, but a fast philosopher may still repeatedly beat a slow neighbour; fairness needs a queue.

notes.title: Other hangs that look like deadlocks
notes.html:
Real incidents are rarely two locks in opposite order. Know these patterns.

  1. Thread pool starvation (self-deadlock). A task running in a pool of 10 threads submits a subtask to the same pool and blocks on its result. If all 10 threads do this, no thread is free to run the subtasks. Fix: separate pools, async composition, or ForkJoinPool which lets a waiting thread help (work stealing).
  2. Lock held across I/O. A thread holds a mutex while calling a slow network service; everyone else stalls for the timeout. Looks like a hang, is really unbounded latency.
  3. Fork and locks. fork() in a multithreaded process copies only the calling thread; if another thread held a lock (even inside malloc), the child's copy of that lock is held forever. Fix: execve right after fork, or use pthread_atfork handlers.
  4. Signal handlers. Calling non-async-signal-safe functions (printf, malloc) inside a handler can self-deadlock on the lock the interrupted code held.
  5. Distributed deadlock. Service A waits for B, B waits for C, C waits for A with synchronous calls and request timeouts of 30 s. Everything times out together; retries amplify the storm. Fix: timeouts decreasing down the chain, circuit breakers, no cyclic call graphs.
  6. Database plus app lock. App takes a Java lock then opens a transaction; another path opens the transaction then takes the lock. Neither the DB nor the JVM sees the cycle, so no detector fires.
  7. Priority inversion (see the concurrency basics note) can look like a hang for the high-priority thread.
$ jstack 2310 | grep -c "pool-1-thread"        # all 10 present
$ jstack 2310 | grep -A4 "pool-1-thread-3"
  java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
    at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(FutureTask.java:191)
    at com.shop.PriceService.compute(PriceService.java:57)

All workers sitting in FutureTask.get is the fingerprint.

Industry examples. Public postmortems frequently cite exhausted connection pools or thread pools with retries creating a metastable failure; Netflix's bulkhead and timeout guidance addresses exactly this.

Everyday analogy. A manager who hires an assistant and then waits for the assistant's report, but the assistant is stuck in a queue behind other managers.

Common interview traps.

  • Restarting the pod and moving on, without taking a thread dump first.
  • Only knowing the "two locks" story; interviewers love the thread-pool self-deadlock.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Deadlock = group waiting in a cycle forever; no CPU use, no error. Find it with jstack, gdb thread dumps, DB deadlock logs.
  • Four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one.
  • Prevention by lock ordering is cheapest and most common; tryLock with timeout and jittered back-off is the second tool; lockdep and TSan find lock-order bugs before production.
  • Avoidance (Banker's algorithm) keeps the system in a safe state but needs advance maximum claims; real systems rarely use it.
  • Detection plus recovery (wait-for graph, kill a victim, retry) is how databases work; apps must retry on deadlock errors.
  • Producer-consumer: bounded buffer with empty, full and mutex semaphores or a blocking queue; bounds give back-pressure.
  • Readers-writers: choose a starvation policy; consider copy-on-write or RCU for read-mostly data.
  • Dining philosophers: order the forks, limit diners to N-1, or use an arbitrator.
  • Many production hangs are pool starvation, locks held over I/O, fork with locks, or cyclic service calls, not classic two-lock deadlocks.
